messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Authority Presence: Police, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Dr. Priya Kapoor

Dr. Priya Kapoor was fifty-one when the assault happened, and forty-eight months later she was still unable to walk past the pharmacy in the basement of her hospital without her chest tightening. The assault itself had occurred in the stairwell of a different hospital, where she had worked as an attending physician in internal medicine. She had stayed late one evening to complete discharge summaries, and when she emerged from her office around nine o'clock, a man she did not initially recognize—a patient she had examined weeks earlier—was waiting on the landing. What followed was a violent attack that lasted perhaps four minutes but had fractured something in Priya that no amount of clinical training had prepared her to repair.

The man had grabbed her from behind, his forearm across her throat, and she had felt the particular hardness of his bicep, the smell of his cologne mixed with sweat, the sound of his breathing in her ear. He had not used a weapon. His hands had been enough. When security finally arrived, he had fled, but the imprint of those hands—the specific shape and temperature of them, the particular angle of his arms—had remained seared into her nervous system. For weeks afterward, any glimpse of a man's forearm, particularly the muscular definition of the bicep, would send her into a state of acute panic. She had come to avoid rolling up her sleeves in public, and she found herself studying the arms of every man who passed her in the hallway at work, cataloguing them, searching for that exact configuration.

In the months following the assault, Priya had developed an elaborate system of avoidance that had quietly reshaped her life. She wore oversized cardigans and long-sleeved jackets even in summer, ostensibly to maintain a professional appearance but actually to feel hidden, to reduce the surface area of her own body that might attract attention. She changed her route home from the hospital three times, each time convinced that the man—though he had been arrested and was in custody—might somehow be waiting for her. The sight of a police officer in the corridor would cause her breathing to shallow; she had come to associate their presence with the assault itself, as though they were harbingers rather than protectors.

What had begun as hypervigilance had evolved into something more corrosive. Priya had lost the ability to trust her colleagues' intentions. A male resident who asked her opinion on a case now seemed to her to be assessing her, measuring her weakness. She questioned whether people were speaking to her because they respected her judgment or because they sensed something broken in her. She had stopped attending the monthly departmental dinners. She had declined a promotion that would have required her to oversee a larger team.

Six months into her recovery, Priya had discovered that gambling provided a peculiar relief. Online poker, slot machines at the casino an hour's drive away—these activities quieted the noise in her mind. The bright lights, the possibility of winning, the pure absorption required to play occupied the space where intrusive thoughts about the assault would otherwise flourish. Over two years, she had lost approximately thirty thousand dollars. Her husband, Rajesh, had discovered the credit card statements and had wept in a way that frightened her more than her own panic attacks did.

The memory itself felt impossible to integrate. When she allowed herself to recall the stairwell—the fluorescent light, the cold concrete wall against her cheek, the smell of industrial cleaner mixed with his cologne—the terror that returned was not a faint echo but a full resurrection. Her body would respond as though it were happening in real time. Yet simultaneously, the memory felt unreal, too extreme to have actually occurred to her, a woman who had spent thirty years in medicine, who had been the one to provide comfort to frightened patients. The contradiction between her sense of herself and what had happened to her had created a kind of cognitive vertigo.

Priya had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that her decades of competence and good judgment had been an illusion, and that people—particularly men she did not know—were inherently dangerous. She no longer attended her temple. She had stopped calling her sister in Vietnam. When she thought about the event, she felt certain she would dissolve, that the terror would consume her entirely, and so she had built an intricate architecture of distraction and avoidance to prevent that thinking from occurring.

It was Rajesh who finally insisted she seek help. He had found her at the casino at two in the morning, and when he brought her home, he had sat on the edge of their bed and told her that he could not watch her disappear any longer. Priya had agreed, not because she believed therapy could repair what had been broken, but because she could no longer bear the weight of pretending to be whole.
